content: Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) was observed in one patient during the first four weeks of therapy. The overall tolerance to the therapy was reported as good. Clofazimine-induced pigmentation was noted in 11 patients, including 2 with paucibacillary (PB) leprosy and 9 with multibacillary (MB) leprosy. This pigmentation gradually regressed over a period of nine months. The study initially included 64 participants, but the final sample size varied due to dropouts. Follow-up assessments were conducted over 24 months, with evaluations at 12, 18, and 24 months. The dropout rate at the end of the follow-up period was not explicitly detailed. The research questions and objectives were clearly stated, and the study population was well-defined. However, the participation rate of eligible individuals was not consistently reported. Inclusion and exclusion criteria were uniformly applied to all participants. In a study by Shen (2012), newly diagnosed MB leprosy patients were treated with uniform multidrug therapy (U-MDT) and followed up annually for three years post-treatment. Outcomes assessed included bacteriological index (BI) and the frequency of reactions. Of the 116 patients initially recruited, 31 dropped out, leaving 89 patients with complete bacteriological data. The follow-up period lasted three years, with assessments conducted annually. In another study by Rao (2009), 64 patients were evaluated for clinical and histopathological improvements, reactions, adverse effects, and therapy tolerance. Among PB patients, two developed dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome, and one developed AGEP within the first four weeks of therapy. Clofazimine pigmentation was observed in 11 patients. Histopathological improvement was noted in most cases, but statistical analysis was limited due to small sample sizes. A systematic review of chemoprophylaxis for leprosy prevention among contacts of leprosy patients identified no studies meeting inclusion criteria for rifampicin-resistant cases. However, single-dose rifampicin (SDR) was found to significantly reduce the incidence of leprosy among close contacts in a large randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in Bangladesh. SDR was also reported to be cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $158 per additional case prevented. Acceptability studies indicated that most contacts were willing to take prophylaxis, though concerns about privacy and stigma were raised. The quality of the RCTs included in the systematic review was generally good. The evidence supported the effectiveness of SDR in reducing leprosy incidence among contacts, with minimal adverse effects reported. However, further research is needed to evaluate its long-term impact and feasibility in programmatic settings.
